title: The effect of the colour temperature of morning light exposure on wellbeing
research_question: This study investigates whether changing the colour temperature of indoor lighting can help improve the health of healthy adults' emotions in life, specifically focusing on the immediate effects of different colour temperatures of morning light on well-being and tympanic temperature, and what parameter range of light is used in the morning to have a lasting effect on mood changes.

participants.description: Healthy adults aged 21-27 years, with an even number of males/females, from the UK (University of Leeds).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: An experimental room with controlled lighting using a ThousLite luminaire system. Test conditions included four correlated colour temperatures (CCT): 2500K, 5000K, 8500K, and 18500K, all at 500lx illuminance, exposed for one hour in the morning. A baseline condition of 3500K at 500lx was used for 15 minutes of adaptation.

measures.instrument: Binaural tympanic membrane temperature (Braun lrt6520 meter)
[PA scores + (100 – NA scores) + KSS score + VAS perceived comfort]/4

findings.mechanism: Light affects body temperature regulation via non-image-forming pathways.
findings.quote: In the ear temperature data on the first day, 2500k, 5000k, 8500k, and 18500k, there were significant differences between ear temperature parameters under light conditions (F43,36; p<0.05).
With the increase of illumination time, except for 2500k, the tympanic temperature under the other three illumination parameters showed a decreasing trend to different degrees.

findings.mechanism: Light CCT affects core body temperature regulation.
findings.quote: There were significant differences in the changes in tympanic temperature under the four lighting parameters (F=43.36, p<0.0001).

findings.mechanism: No differential effect on thermoregulation between very high CCTs.
findings.quote: Although there is no significant difference between 8500k and 18000k (p=0.7223).

findings.antecedent: 2500K light (low CCT) vs 5000K, 8500K, or 18000K light (higher CCTs)
findings.mechanism: Low CCT light has a distinct effect on thermoregulation compared to higher CCTs.
findings.quote: There were significant differences between 2500k (low colour temperature) and 5000k or 8500k (high colour temperature), 18000k (extremely high colour temperature) (p=0.0002; p=0.0117; p=0.0014).

findings.mechanism: Visually warm low CCT light may affect body temperature.
findings.quote: Moreover, this upward trend can also be seen in Figure 4.

findings.mechanism: Low CCT light can induce feelings of sleepiness.
findings.quote: 2500k light can make people feel sleepy, but there is a slight increase in tympanic temperature.

findings.mechanism: Core body temperature and sleepiness level interact.
findings.quote: A strong correlation was also found between tympanic temperature and KSS score under the four different light parameters, confirming that core body temperature and sleepiness level interacted with each other.

findings.mechanism: Higher CCT light (8500K) promotes alertness more effectively than lower CCT light (2500K).
findings.quote: ANOVA revealed a significant difference between the 2500k and 8500k conditions, with scores in the 8500k condition significantly lower than those in the 2500k condition (lower KSS scores mean higher alertness).

findings.mechanism: Higher CCTs tend to reduce sleepiness, but the difference between very high CCTs and moderate CCTs may not be statistically significant.
findings.quote: The KSS scores for both the 8500k and 18000k conditions were lower than those for the 2500k and 5000k conditions, although these differences did not reach statistical significance (p>0.05).

findings.mechanism: High CCT light can enhance positive emotions.
findings.quote: except for the positive change of emotional PA-P under the condition of 8500k light in the morning, the results of other light parameters showed no noticeable activation effect.

findings.mechanism: Positive affect increases with CCT up to a certain point (around 8500K), beyond which it does not continuously improve.
findings.quote: It can be seen from the score of PANAS-P that with the increase in colour temperature, PANAS-P has a positive effect. However, it will not improve because of the continuous increase in colour temperature. It will reach a relative peak at around 8500k

findings.mechanism: High CCT light can reduce negative emotions.
findings.quote: 8500k also has an obvious weakening effect on NA at the same time.

findings.antecedent: Light conditions and time of exposure
findings.mechanism: Both the CCT of light and the duration of exposure influence mood.
findings.quote: Regarding the mood scale, we observed that 'light conditions' and 'time' had significant effects when looking at the entire course of the experiment.

findings.mechanism: Moderate to high CCTs significantly improve positive affect.
findings.quote: The PANAS changes under the 5000k, and 8500k lighting parameters showed a significant positive increase.

findings.mechanism: Optimal CCT can positively influence overall wellbeing by affecting mood, alertness, and physical comfort.
findings.quote: In the current data, 8500k has the most positive impact on the human body's comprehensive factors, but the threshold range has not been determined.

findings.antecedent: 8500K lighting parameter vs 5000K and 18000K lighting conditions
findings.mechanism: While 8500K positively affects mood and alertness, its effect on physical comfort may not be superior to other CCTs.
findings.quote: However, the physical comfort under this lighting parameter is not as high as the 5000k lighting condition and the 18000k lighting condition, as can be seen from the values for mood and alertness; these factors were not continuously optimised as the lighting parameters continued to increase.

findings.consequent: Human mood, alertness, and physical comfort
findings.mechanism: Morning light exposure has a general positive impact on various aspects of wellbeing.
findings.quote: This study provides evidence that morning light does improve human mood to some extent and is also associated with alertness and physical comfort.

mechanisms: Light affects the hypothalamus, which regulates visceral activity, body temperature, feeding behaviour, water balance, endocrine functions, experience response, and biological rhythms.
Core body temperature and sleepiness level interact.
Alertness, sleepiness, and melatonin secretion correlate with tympanic temperature.
implementation_implications: It is questionable whether universal lighting solutions are suitable for the use of lower CCT in daily life.
Morning light does improve human mood to some extent and is also associated with alertness and physical comfort.
8500K CCT has the most positive impact on comprehensive wellbeing factors, but the precise threshold range needs further determination.
limitations: The method chosen for assessing circadian rhythm (not using melatonin collection or actigraphy) might be inappropriate or too stressful for participants.
The timing and duration of light exposure may affect the results.
The experiment schedule was set at the same time in the morning, potentially limiting generalizability.
Significant individual differences in circadian rhythms due to age and gender suggest that universal lighting solutions may not be suitable for all populations.
The threshold range for optimal CCT has not been determined.
